title: Fall Around Phoenixville: Pumpkin Patches, Hayrides, Haunts and Foliage
seo_title: Fall Things to Do Near Phoenixville, PA (2026)
description: Pumpkin patches, hayrides, corn mazes, apple picking, the Halloween parade and haunted attractions near Phoenixville, PA, with 2026 dates and prices.

sections.heading: How the season runs here
sections.html:
There are more fall things to do around Phoenixville than one October can hold, and the season has a rhythm worth knowing before you plan weekends around it. The farm stands and pumpkin patches open in the second half of September and most of them close the weekend after Halloween. October is when the borough leans into Halloween: the Colonial Theatre programs horror all month, the parade shuts down Bridge Street, and the haunted attractions across the river run every weekend. Leaves peak late in this corner of Pennsylvania, usually the last week of October into the first week of November, so the best hikes come after the pumpkins are gone. And the whole thing ends in December when the town burns a giant wooden bird.

Everything below is within roughly a half hour of downtown unless noted. Dates are for 2026 where the venues have published them; a few still show last year's schedule, and we say so.

sections.heading: Colonial Gardens: Pumpkinland, right in town
sections.html:
The closest thing Phoenixville has to a fall tradition is Colonial Gardens, the family-run nursery on Schuylkill Road that has been throwing an October party for more than forty years. Every fall the back lot becomes Pumpkinland: cartoon-character cutouts, scarecrows, hay hutches and, by their count, more than ten tons of pumpkins. Walking through the display is free, which makes it the easy default for a Sunday afternoon with small kids.

2026 daytime season: September 19 through November 1, 10am to 4:30pm daily, weather permitting. The paid pieces are cheap: the Enchanted Hayride is $10, each of the three mazes (Cornstalk Maze, Halloween Funhouse and Casper's Castle) is $5, and a combo ticket covering the hayride and mazes is $13. Kids two and under are free with a paying adult.

After dark the tone changes. On October weekends the same hayride becomes a Haunted Hayride and Hedge Maze, recommended for ages eight and up, and on select weeknights they run a milder Children's Night Hayride for families who want the flashlights without the chainsaws. As of early September the site still lists 2025's night dates (Friday to Sunday nights for the haunt, midweek for the kids' version), so check before you go.

Go early on Saturdays. The lot on Schuylkill Road is not big and the mums-and-pumpkins shoppers compete with the hayride crowd. 745 Schuylkill Road, Phoenixville (map).

sections.heading: Yeagers Farm: the local produce stop
sections.html:
Out on Route 113, Yeagers Farm & Market is the working farm a lot of locals use without thinking of it as an attraction. The family has farmed here for over two centuries. Summer is sweet corn and tomatoes; in fall the stand switches to pumpkins, apples, cider, mums and decor, with weekend hayrides out to the pumpkin patch and a corn maze on the property. It's smaller and quieter than the ticketed farms below, which is exactly why some people prefer it, and the pumpkin prices reflect that it's a farm rather than a theme park. The Friday after Thanksgiving it turns into a Christmas tree lot.

1015 Pikesprings Road, Phoenixville (map). Call 610-935-8244 for weekend hayride hours.

sections.heading: Arader Farm: Collegeville's fall weekends
sections.html:
Ten minutes up Route 29, Arader Farm is the place many people still call Varner's. The Arader family bought the Varner Christmas tree farm in 2021 and kept the fall operation going, so if an older listing sends you to Varner Farms on South Trappe Road, this is it.

2026 fall season opens September 24. Hours are Thursday and Friday noon to 6pm, Saturday 10am to 6pm and Sunday 10am to 5pm. Tractor rides run straight to the pumpkin patch, and the grounds have a corn maze, a model train, a barnyard of "farm friends", a play area they call Honeybee Hay Land, and a fall store for cider and decor. A food truck starts September 26, and the Troubles End biergarten pours on weekend afternoons.

The two big days are Pumpkin Fest, October 10 and 17, when the farm runs its full slate of pony rides, pumpkin painting, face painting and scarecrow making. Parking is free. Leave the dog at home; they are strict about it. When the pumpkins are gone the farm flips to Christmas trees, and its Walking Wonderland light show opens November 20.

746 South Trappe Road, Collegeville (map).

sections.heading: Merrymead Farm: the big one, with the ice cream
sections.html:
Merrymead Farm in Worcester Township is the biggest fall production within easy reach, and the reason to make the twenty-five minute drive is that it's a real dairy: you finish the corn maze and walk into a store that makes its own ice cream. The season kicks off in late September with the Lighting of the Great Pumpkin, then Fall Harvest Days run every weekend in October (October 3-4, 10-11, 17-18, 24-25 and 31 in 2026), Saturdays 11am to 5pm and Sundays noon to 5pm.

Admission covers a five-acre corn maze, hayrides, a jump pad, a barrel train, a corn bin, a cornstalk tunnel, a haystack pyramid and the farm animals. Apple cannons and gem mining cost extra. Last year the gate was $25 (or $22 booked online) for Harvest Days, and the Moonlight Maze on Thursday, Friday and Saturday evenings was $19 at the gate or $16 online; bring a flashlight, and note the last hayride leaves at 8:45pm. Anyone under 16 needs an adult with them. Every activity is outdoors and weather-dependent, so a rainy Saturday means a closed farm.

2222 South Valley Forge Road, Lansdale (map).

sections.heading: More farms worth the drive
sections.html:
• Northern Star Farm, Trappe — 15 minutes. The 18th annual Fall Fest runs September 13 to October 26, Saturdays and Sundays 10am to 5pm: a seven-acre corn maze, hayrides, pony rides, apple slingshots, a play barn and, crucially, hot apple cider donuts. 96 Third Avenue East (map). northernstarfarm.net
  • Milky Way Farm, Chester Springs — 15 minutes. The cheapest ticket on this list: $5 admission, $4 hayride, September 26 through October 31, Saturdays and Sundays 10am to 5pm plus Friday afternoons. Pick your own pumpkins, walk a corn maze, then get ice cream from the dairy. 521 East Uwchlan Avenue on Route 113 (map).
  • Highland Orchards, West Chester — 30 minutes. The apple-picking pick. Pick-your-own runs Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 3pm, through October (McIntosh are in now), and fall weekends add a corn maze, apple cannons, hayrides and a beer garden with food trucks. 1000 Marshallton-Thorndale Road (map). highlandorchards.net
  • Frecon Farms, Boyertown — 30 minutes. Pick your own from more than 25 apple varieties, then taste the hard cider they ferment from them at the estate cidery. The scratch bakery is the other reason to go. 501 South Reading Avenue (map).
  • Hopewell Furnace, Elverson — 30 minutes. A National Park Service iron plantation where, in season, you can pick heirloom apple varieties from the historic orchard for a small fee. Quiet, uncrowded and pretty. Call 610-582-8773 to check what's ripe. (map)
  • Linvilla Orchards, Media — 45 minutes. The region's giant. Pumpkinland runs September 12 through November 8 with no admission charge; you pay per activity (hayrides $9, mazes $7, the Hayride to the Witch's House $13 online). Worth a full day once, especially with visiting relatives. linvilla.com

sections.heading: Halloween in the borough
sections.html:
The Spirit of Phoenixville Halloween Parade & Trunk or Treat is the night the town shows up in costume. The parade steps off from the Borough Hall lot and comes down Bridge Street to Church Street Alley, and the 100 block of Bridge, between Church Alley and Starr Street, closes for trunk-or-treat afterward. In past years registration opened at 5pm with judging at 6 and the parade at 7. The Borough hasn't posted the 2026 date yet as of early September; it lands in the back half of October, and the Borough calendar is where it will appear first.

The Colonial Theatre treats October the way it treats July: as an excuse. Among the 2026 dates:

  • October 8 — History on the Rocks: Haunted Phoenixville, local ghost stories with a drink in hand.
  • October 21 — the Italian prog band Goblin plays its score live to Dario Argento's Tenebre.
  • October 28 — Haunted Halloween Shorts, locally written spooky plays from the Parlour Reading Series.
  • All month — a horror series that runs from Night of the Living Dead (October 7) through Hocus Pocus (October 16), Halloween (October 23), The Nightmare Before Christmas (October 24), Nosferatu (October 25) and The Exorcist on Halloween night.
  • October 31 — the first Phoenixville Halloween Bash, 8pm to midnight, hosted by Mayor Peter Urscheler: performances, immersive rooms, a costume contest and specialty drinks. Costumes are mandatory, not suggested.

Pennhurst Asylum is the serious haunt, and it's five minutes across the river in Spring City on the grounds of the real, notorious state institution, which is most of why it works. The 2026 season opens September 25 and runs Fridays and Saturdays through November 7, adding Sundays in October, with a final Blackout weekend November 6-7. Tickets are timed and sold online only; the box office opens at 6:30pm. Not for young kids, and not for anyone who dislikes being touched by a stranger in the dark. pennhurstasylum.com

Further afield, the Great Pumpkin Carve in Chadds Ford (about 45 minutes) is October 15-17: more than seventy giant pumpkins carved by local artists on Thursday, then lit in a meadow on Friday and Saturday nights with live music, food, beer and wine. It photographs better than anything else on this page. No dogs.

sections.heading: Where to see the leaves
sections.html:
Southeastern Pennsylvania peaks late, typically between the last week of October and the first week of November. That's after most of the farms close, so treat foliage as its own season.

  • Black Rock Sanctuary — a mile north of downtown on Route 113, 119 acres of former silt basin turned wetland and meadow, with a paved 0.9-mile interpretive loop that's stroller- and wheelchair-friendly. It sits on the Atlantic flyway, so October brings migrating waterfowl and, most evenings, hawks and the occasional eagle over the river. (map)
  • Schuylkill River Trail — the section from the Phoenixville trailhead toward Mont Clare and Port Providence runs along the water under a canopy that turns all at once. Flat, so it's the bike option.
  • Valley Forge — the five-mile Joseph Plumb Martin loop passes every monument and meadow in the park. Go on a weekday morning; the Sunday crowd is real.
  • Bryn Coed Preserve, Chester Springs — Natural Lands' 1,500 acres of former farmland, free and open sunrise to sunset (closed Thursdays). The one-mile loop to the Peacock Oak, one of the largest white oaks in Pennsylvania, is the short version; the meadow trails are the long one. (map)
  • French Creek State Park and Hopewell Furnace — the deep-woods choice, 30 minutes west, with lakes, hemlock ravines and a lot more mileage than anything closer to town.

sections.heading: Dates to circle
sections.html:
• September 5-6 — Phoenixville Vintage Fest, Bridge and Main Street lot, 9am to 4pm.
  • September 5-7 — Ludwig's Corner Horse Show & Country Fair, Glenmoore. The 83rd edition: jumpers, a midway, a vendor village and a beer garden over the main ring. $10 a car, free after 4pm.
  • September 17-20 — Phoenixville Film Festival at the Colonial, 62 films including four world premieres.
  • September 19 — Upper Providence's free Community Fall Festival in Collegeville: hayrides, pony rides, a petting zoo, food trucks and a beer garden.
  • October 3 — Chester County Day, the 85th annual house tour. This year's route covers the county's northwest quadrant, which is our corner; expect to see historic homes you drive past every week.
  • October 10 and 17 — Pumpkin Fest at Arader Farm.
  • October 15-17 — Great Pumpkin Carve, Chadds Ford.
  • October 31 — Halloween Bash at the Colonial.
  • December 12 — the Firebird Festival, 601 Franklin Avenue from 4pm, free. The town builds a wooden phoenix all fall and burns it at dusk. Technically winter; spiritually, the end of this list.
Three practical things. Buy farm tickets online, where most of them are a few dollars cheaper and some weekends sell out. Every farm on this page closes for rain, so check social media the morning of. And the cider donut hierarchy, for what it's worth: Northern Star, then Highland, then Linvilla. Argue with us on the community board.

title: The Complete Guide to Blobfest
description: Phoenixville throws a three-day party for a fictional monster every July. The 1958 film shot down the street, the fire extinguisher parade, the Run-Out, how to get tickets, and when the next one lands.

sections.heading: Why a Pennsylvania borough throws a party for a monster
sections.html:
In 1958, a low-budget sci-fi picture called The Blob filmed its most famous scene inside Phoenixville's Colonial Theatre: a packed house of moviegoers bursting through the doors onto Bridge Street to escape a creeping, man-eating goo. The shot lasts seconds. Phoenixville has been re-enacting it for a quarter century.

The Colonial opened in 1903 and, like most single-screen movie houses, spent the back half of the century sliding toward demolition. A nonprofit bought and restored it in the late 1990s, and rather than downplay the building's B-movie past, they leaned all the way in. The first Blobfest ran in 2000. The 2026 edition was the 27th. It now fills the theatre and shuts down several blocks of downtown for a full weekend every July.

sections.heading: The movie they shot down the street
sections.html:
Most of The Blob was made within a few miles of where the festival happens. Production was based at Valley Forge Studios, with location work scattered across Chester Springs, Downingtown, Royersford and Phoenixville itself — Doc Hallen's house and garage were local, and the diner the Blob engulfs was the Downingtown Diner, which stood at 81 West Lancaster Avenue about twelve miles southwest of town.

The Colonial got into the film almost by accident. The crew needed somewhere to screen their dailies, the theatre had the projectors, and the building talked its way into the movie's signature sequence.

Two bits of trivia worth having: this was Steve McQueen's first starring role, and he was pushing thirty while playing a teenager. And the celebrated shot of the Blob oozing over the diner was done by mounting a still photograph of the building on a gyroscopic table, letting a batch of the goo roll off it, and printing the negative in reverse.

sections.heading: The Fire Extinguisher Parade
sections.html:
Blobfest opens not with a screening but with a procession of people carrying fire extinguishers down Bridge Street to the theatre doors — where, on cue, they let them off all at once in a white cloud that organizers cheerfully describe as the town's version of daytime fireworks.

It is a straight-faced tribute to the plot. In the film nothing stops the creature until the characters discover it recoils from cold, and the town empties its supply of CO₂ extinguishers — pooled from the fire department and the local high school — to freeze the thing solid. The parade was dreamed up by artist Andee Miskiewicz, who also designed the Blob plaque that hangs inside the Colonial.

It is free, it happens in the street, and it is the single most photographed thing at the festival after the Run-Out. If you are only coming for an hour, come for this.

sections.heading: The Run-Out: the main event
sections.html:
The centerpiece is the Run-Out, a live re-creation of the 1958 escape: several hundred costumed people screaming their way out of the Colonial's doors while thousands watch from Bridge Street. Participants are inside for a pre-show first, so the ticket buys you the whole experience rather than ten seconds of sprinting.

Only about 350 Run-Out tickets exist, and in recent years they have sold out within minutes of going on sale.

Ticket tip: tickets typically go on sale in the spring, months ahead of the July weekend. Follow the Colonial's Blobfest page and their social accounts for the on-sale announcement, set a reminder, and be at your keyboard the minute it opens. If you miss out, watching from the street costs nothing and is genuinely the better view.

sections.heading: What happens each day
sections.html:
Each year runs under a theme — 2026 was Cirque du Blobfest, a carnival treatment complete with a ringmaster-led pre-show; 2025 was Camp Blobfest; 2023 was Blobs and Monsters. The bones of the weekend stay the same.

  • Friday night — the fire extinguisher parade kicks things off, followed by the costume contest, the scream contest, the Run-Out, and an immersive screening of The Blob that has drifted toward Rocky Horror territory: callbacks, audience participation, staged interruptions.
  • Saturday — the street fair takes over Bridge Street with vendors, artists, live entertainment and family activities, running alongside a full day of programming inside the theatre: genre screenings, a short-film contest, and guests.
  • Sunday — the Blobfest 5K, 10K, Half Marathon and Kids Fun Run, hosted by the RUNegades and now nearly a decade old. Proceeds go back to the nonprofit theatre.

sections.heading: Practical tips
sections.html:
• Parking. Downtown lots fill early on Blobfest Saturday. Park several blocks out and walk in, or arrive well before midday.
  • What costs money. The street fair and the fire extinguisher parade are free. Screenings, contests and the Run-Out are ticketed through the Colonial's site and sell out at very different speeds — Run-Out first, screenings not far behind.
  • Costumes. Welcome everywhere, all weekend, not just during the contest. Nobody will look at you sideways for showing up covered in red goo.
  • Heat. This is an outdoor July festival in southeastern Pennsylvania. Water, shade and sunscreen matter more than people expect.
  • Make a night of it. Bridge Street's restaurants and breweries are steps from the theatre, and several are BYOB — see our BYOB guide. Book ahead; the whole downtown is busy that weekend.

sections.heading: When is the next Blobfest?
sections.html:
Blobfest lands on the second weekend of July. The next one is July 9–11, 2027, at the Colonial Theatre on Bridge Street. The theme and lineup are usually announced in the spring, with Run-Out tickets going on sale around the same time.

Watch the LocalSpot events calendar — every Blobfest event appears there as soon as the Colonial announces it.

title: Every BYOB in Phoenixville, Ranked
description: Phoenixville is quietly one of the best BYOB towns in the Philly suburbs. Here's every bring-your-own spot we know, ranked by what each does best.

sections.heading: The ranking
sections.html:
1. Il Granaio — the classic Phoenixville BYOB. Intimate Italian on Bridge Street with housemade pasta and locally sourced ingredients. Bring a good red and book ahead; this is the date-night pick. (map)
  2. Avlós Greek Cuisine — fresh lamb, whole fish, and Mediterranean plates in a sunny Bridge Street room. Works equally well for a romantic dinner or a loud group; a crisp white is the move. (map)
  3. Sage Mediterranean — the casual one. Hummus, kebabs, and falafel in a cozy space at friendlier prices; great for a low-key weeknight bottle. (map)
  4. Tai Me Up — downtown Thai that welcomes your bottle; a dry Riesling next to a curry is one of the best pairings in town. (map)
  5. Black Lab Bistro — upscale-casual New American with a seasonal menu. It ranks lower only because it's the fanciest room on the list, which makes the BYOB feel like a cheat code: white-tablecloth cooking, your own wine. (map)

sections.heading: Also mentioned around town
sections.html: Diners and local lists also cite Dante's Italian Bistro & Pastry, Vecchia Nuova, and Bella Trattoria as BYOB-friendly. We haven't verified their current policies, so call before you carry.

sections.heading: BYOB ground rules
sections.html:
• Policies change. A quick call ahead saves an awkward table moment — some spots limit you to wine and beer, and a few charge a small corkage fee.
  • Chill it yourself. Most BYOBs will happily provide glasses and an opener, but don't count on fridge space for your white.
  • Buy local first: Bluebird Distilling and the bottle shops on Bridge Street make it easy to pick something up on the walk over.

Want these on a map? The LocalSpot dining tab has a BYOB filter and a map view of every spot in town.
